summary: The job ends: The job ends, and {the first to hear} asks what the household does now.
realLife: One life: A Boston writer told in a routine morning meeting that her position was eliminated. Her email was cut off within minutes. About a dozen people were affected, seniority did not protect anyone, and it was her second layoff in three years. Another: A communications specialist on a contract with a federal aid agency whose layoff email came in the middle of the night. She had two days of health insurance left, a day to return equipment and no severance. She had told her father and close friends her fears beforehand and then leaned on laid-off colleagues in group chats. Another: A counterterrorism expert with twelve years in his agency, cut by a form email while working from home. He describes anxiety and depression afterward. Many former colleagues applied for hundreds of jobs without offers, and some took service work when benefits ran out. Another: He lost his job when a carmaker closed its Moraine, Ohio, plant in 2008. By 2010 the couple were struggling with unemployment and had lost their health insurance. He later became an electrician at another plant and kept up photography. Another: An assembly-line worker who learned of her plant's planned closure from a television announcement the night before it was public. The next day coworkers were split between accepting it and feeling slighted, and transfers were offered. The job had carried her from homelessness to owning a home.
